theme: Cities of refuge; warfare; difficult cases
readingInstruction: Read Deuteronomy 19:1-21:23. These chapters deal with cities of refuge, witnesses, warfare, and a series of difficult cases. Read them slowly. Some are hard, and they should be understood in the context of ancient Israel as a nation under the old covenant.
settingTheScene: Moses continues applying the law to civil life. He repeats the provision for cities of refuge, stresses the need for honest witnesses, sets out rules for warfare, and addresses a series of specific situations: an unsolved murder, a captive woman, the rights of the firstborn, a rebellious son, and the body of an executed criminal. These cases show how the law dealt with the real complications of community life.
observation: Three cities of refuge are to be set apart, with roads prepared and room for three more if the territory expands (19:1-10).
“A single witness shall not suffice… only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established” (19:15).
A false witness is to receive the punishment that he intended for the accused (19:16-21).
Before battle, the priest is to say, “Hear, O Israel, today you are drawing near for battle against your enemies: let not your heart faint. Do not fear” (20:1-4).
Those who are afraid, newly married, or have just built a house are excused from battle (20:5-9).
When a corpse is found in the field, the elders of the nearest city must wash their hands and say, “Our hands did not shed this blood” (21:1-9).
Firstborn sons have a right to a double portion, even if their father prefers another wife’s son (21:15-17).
“A hanged man is cursed by God,” and his body must not remain overnight on the tree (21:22-23).
interpretation:
These chapters show that Israel’s law was not a code of rigid rules but a system for taking human life, truth, and community seriously. The cities of refuge protect the innocent. The rule of two or three witnesses protects the accused. The penalty for false witnesses, to receive what they meant for others, is a strict deterrent. Together, they show a concern for justice that was remarkable in the ancient world.

Notice the tenderness of the rules of war. A priest tells the soldiers not to be afraid, because “the LORD your God is he who goes with you.” Men who have just married or built a house are sent home, so that they do not die before enjoying what they have started. Even the fearful are released, so that their fear does not spread. This is not the rhetoric of a war machine. It is a view of war as a grave and limited matter.

The case of the unsolved murder is a striking picture of communal responsibility. When someone is found dead and no one knows who killed him, the nearest town is responsible for making atonement. The elders wash their hands over a heifer whose neck is broken, and pray, “Forgive, O LORD, your people Israel.” It shows that bloodshed pollutes a community, and that someone must acknowledge it.

The rule about the firstborn protects a son from the favoritism of a father. Even the unloved wife’s son has his rights. God’s law is concerned with fairness inside the family.

The last verse, 21:23, is the most important for what comes later. A body hanged on a tree was cursed, and it was to be buried by sundown, so that the land would not be defiled. The person was cursed “by God.” It was a mark of the deepest shame. The New Testament sees this as a description of what Christ would bear.
connection: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 21:23 in Galatians 3:13: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.” Peter says that Jesus “bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). The requirement of two or three witnesses is quoted by Jesus (Matthew 18:16) and Paul (2 Corinthians 13:1). The cities of refuge point to Christ as our refuge (Hebrews 6:18). Jesus told his disciples, “Do not be afraid,” as he sent them out.
application:
Think about how you treat people in disputes. Are you fair and honest in what you say about them?

Read Galatians 3:13 and thank Christ for taking the curse in your place.

If there is fear in your heart, hear the priest’s words from 20:4: “The LORD your God is he who goes with you.”
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for becoming a curse for you on the tree.
Ask God to make you honest and fair in your dealings.
Ask him to go with you into the battles you face.
